[SUMMARY]  
**Clinical Summary:**  
A newborn presents with **early-onset bilious vomiting**, beginning on day 1 of life — a critical sign of **high-grade intestinal obstruction**. Abdominal examination demonstrates **upper abdominal distension with relative lower abdominal concavity**, and auscultation reveals **normal bowel sounds**, consistent with a **proximal obstruction**. The **abdominal radiograph shows the classic “double bubble” sign**, confirming **duodenal atresia** — a failure of duodenal lumen recanalization, typically at the level of the ampulla of Vater.

Supporting dysmorphic features include **epicanthal folds** and **upslanting palpebral fissures**, and a **grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur** at the left mid-to-lower sternal border raises concern for **congenital heart disease**, commonly associated with **Trisomy 21**. Duodenal atresia is strongly linked to Down syndrome (~30–40% prevalence), and cardiac anomalies (e.g., AV canal defects) frequently co-occur.

No prenatal ultrasound findings were reported, though polyhydramnios and fetal bowel dilation are common antenatal clues. Chromosomal testing has not been confirmed, but **karyotype or chromosomal microarray is urgently indicated**. An **echocardiogram is mandatory** prior to surgical intervention to evaluate for structural heart disease.

**Immediate next steps:**  
- **NPO status and nasogastric tube placement** for gastric decompression  
- **Electrolyte panel, renal function tests, and blood gas** to assess for dehydration, electrolyte derangements, or metabolic acidosis  
- **Urgent pediatric surgery consultation** — definitive management is **surgical correction** (e.g., duodenoduodenostomy)  
- **Genetic counseling and confirmatory genetic testing**  
- **Echocardiography before surgery**  

This presentation represents a **surgical emergency** requiring prompt diagnosis and coordinated multidisciplinary care.

[THOUGHT]  
The case describes a newborn with classic, pathognomonic findings of duodenal atresia: early-onset bilious vomiting (day 1), upper abdominal distension with relative lower abdominal concavity (suggesting obstruction proximal to the ligament of Treitz), normal bowel sounds (preserved proximal motility), and — most definitively — the “double bubble” sign on abdominal radiograph. This radiographic finding reflects air in the dilated stomach and proximal duodenum, with no distal gas, confirming a high-grade proximal small bowel obstruction. The associated dysmorphic features (epicanthal folds, upslanting palpebral fissures) and congenital heart murmur strongly support an underlying chromosomal disorder, with Trisomy 21 being the most common and well-established association — ~30–40% of infants with duodenal atresia have Down syndrome, and AV canal defects are the most frequent cardiac anomaly. All other elements (polyhydramnios not reported but consistent with antenatal presentation; need for pre-op echo, karyotype, NG decompression, urgent surgery) align precisely with standard-of-care for duodenal atresia. No contradictory findings are present (e.g., no evidence of malrotation with volvulus — which would show abnormal rotation or “corkscrew” duodenum, or absent bowel sounds; no pneumatosis or portal venous gas to suggest NEC; no distal obstruction signs like lower abdominal distension or meconium ileus pattern). Thus, the diagnosis is definitive based on imaging and clinical presentation.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Early-onset bilious vomiting beginning on day 1 of life  
- Upper abdominal distension with relative lower abdominal concavity  
- Normal bowel sounds on auscultation  
- Abdominal radiograph showing the classic “double bubble” sign  
- Epicanthal folds and upslanting palpebral fissures (dysmorphic features associated with Trisomy 21)  
- Grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur at left mid-to-lower sternal border (suggestive of AV canal defect, commonly seen in Down syndrome)  
- Duodenal atresia explicitly stated as due to failure of duodenal lumen recanalization at the ampulla of Vater  
- Strong epidemiologic link between duodenal atresia and Trisomy 21 (~30–40% prevalence)  

[GAPS]  
- Karyotype or chromosomal microarray results are pending/unconfirmed  
- Echocardiogram findings are not yet available  
- Prenatal ultrasound findings (e.g., polyhydramnios, fetal bowel dilation) were not reported  
- Serum electrolytes, renal function, and blood gas values are not provided  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Duodenal atresia
